design.title: Web design
design.desc: Interfaces that look sharp and convert — from landing pages to full product design.
design.intro: Design here means working out what a page is for before deciding what it looks like. We start from the people visiting the site and the action you need them to take, then design the shortest honest path between the two. Every layout is tested in a real browser at phone and desktop widths before it is called finished.

deliverables.1: Wireframes for the pages that carry the load
deliverables.2: UI design in Figma, desktop and mobile
deliverables.4: Design tokens ready for the build

process.0: Research: who visits, what they need, what competitors do.
process.1: Structure: sitemap, page outlines and the copy each page needs.
process.2: Design: interface, type and motion, reviewed as working pages.
process.3: Handover: tokens and components the build uses directly.

goodFor.0: Marketing sites that need to explain and sell
goodFor.2: Redesigns of sites that look dated or convert poorly

0.a: Yes. Wireframes and UI live in Figma, and you get the file. Because we also build the site, the design is reviewed as working pages in a browser from the second week, not only as flat screens.

1.q: Can you design only, and hand it to another developer?
1.a: Yes. The handover includes tokens, components and a specification. Most clients keep design and build in one place with us, because it removes the gap where things get lost.

2.q: Do you write the copy too?
2.a: We structure it and write the first draft for the pages we design, in English or Greek. Final wording is reviewed with you.

development.title: Development
development.desc: Fast, accessible builds in modern frameworks, shipped and maintained end to end.
development.intro: We build with Next.js, React and TypeScript, with content in a headless CMS such as Sanity so your team edits pages, products and prices without a developer. Every site ships with the technical SEO in place: semantic HTML, metadata and structured data per page and per language, fast loading on a phone, and accessibility checked before launch.

deliverables.0: Front-end build in Next.js and TypeScript
deliverables.1: Headless CMS set-up and editor training
deliverables.3: Forms, booking flows and third-party integrations
deliverables.4: Hosting on Vercel, analytics and launch checklist

process.0: Set-up: repository, hosting, CMS schema and the design tokens.
process.1: Build: pages go live on a preview URL in weekly increments.
process.2: Content: your team loads real content while the build continues.
process.3: Launch: performance, SEO and accessibility pass, then the domain switch.

goodFor.0: Bilingual websites for businesses in Greece
goodFor.3: Web apps with accounts, dashboards and maps

0.a: Speed, security and control. A Next.js site is pre-rendered, so pages load instantly and rank better on Core Web Vitals, and there is no plugin layer to patch. Editors still get a friendly CMS for content.

1.q: Can my team update the site without you?
1.a: Yes. Pages, text, images, products and prices are edited in the CMS. Publishing a new car on the Marvel Cars site takes the team about five minutes.

2.q: Who hosts the site and what does it cost?
2.a: Sites run on Vercel, on your own account so you own everything. Most sites fit within the free or the lowest paid tier; the CMS has a free tier too.

3.q: Do you maintain sites after launch?
3.a: Yes. Launch includes a handover, and the ongoing partner engagement reserves monthly capacity for updates, new pages and performance work.

brand.title: Brand systems
brand.desc: Design systems and identity work that keep every surface consistent as you grow.
brand.intro: A brand system is the set of rules that makes every surface, from the website to a social post, look like it comes from the same company. We define the identity where one is missing, and where one exists we turn it into a design system: type, colour, spacing, components and the guidelines that keep new work consistent.

deliverables.0: Logo use, type and colour definitions
deliverables.2: Templates for social posts and presentations
deliverables.3: Written guidelines for your team and future suppliers

process.0: Audit: everything that carries the brand today, and where it breaks.
process.1: Define: the few rules that matter, written down and shown in use.
process.2: Apply: the website and the templates built on the same tokens.
process.3: Hand over: guidelines plus the working files.

goodFor.0: Companies whose website and materials have drifted apart
goodFor.1: Startups launching with a new identity
goodFor.2: Teams that produce content in-house and need templates
goodFor.3: Rebrands that need to land on the website first

0.a: As part of an identity for a web project, yes. We do not take on logo-only work; the value of a brand system is in applying it consistently, which starts with the site.

1.q: We already have a brand book. Is this still useful?
1.a: Usually. A brand book covers print and logo use; a design system covers the web: components, states, spacing and motion. We build the second on top of the first.

discovery.name: Discovery sprint
discovery.body: A fixed-scope fortnight to work out what should actually be built. You come away with a sitemap, a content model, wireframes for the pages that carry the load, and a build estimate that holds up.

build.name: Design and build
build.body: The full engagement. Design and code advance together in weekly increments, so you are reviewing working pages in a browser from week two rather than approving flat comps and hoping.

partner.name: Ongoing partner
partner.body: A standing allocation for teams that ship continuously. Campaign pages, new sections, performance work and the accumulated small things that never quite justify their own project.

Marvelcars.title: 27 luxury cars, picked and reserved in minutes
Marvelcars.summary: A bilingual rental site for Marvel Cars Athens: fleet, day rates and handover points laid out so a visitor picks a car and reserves it in minutes.
Marvelcars.challenge: Marvel Cars hires out 27 luxury and performance cars from three points on the Athens Riviera, and most customers arrive by plane or ferry and book from a phone. The site had to show the right car, its real all-in price and where to collect it in two languages, without a developer in the loop every time the fleet changed.

approach.0: Modelled the fleet in Sanity so cars, categories, day rates and photos are edited by the team, not by us.
approach.1: Grouped the fleet into SUVs, sportscars and daily rentals, with VAT, collision cover and liability shown in the price up front.
approach.2: Built the whole site in English and Greek, with its own route and metadata per language.
approach.3: Added landing pages for airport arrivals, ferry ports, the Riviera, weddings and corporate hire, each ending in the same reservation flow.

1.label: Time to publish a new car

Karatheodoris.title: Two museums, a dance school and a calendar, in two languages
Karatheodoris.summary: A bilingual site for the Cultural Association of Nea Vyssa «Stefanos Karatheodoris»: its events, its two museums and online booking for the Folklore Museum, in Greek and English.
Karatheodoris.challenge: Since 1977 the association has kept the memory of the Karatheodoris family and the traditions of Nea Vyssa alive, through the Carathéodory Museum, the Folklore Museum, three dance departments and a year-round programme of events. Visitors come from Greece and abroad, so everything had to read in both languages, the volunteers running it needed to post events and change the homepage themselves, and museum visits had to be bookable online.

approach.0: Built the whole site in Greek and English, with its own route and metadata per language.
approach.1: Modelled events and the homepage slides in Sanity, so the association publishes its calendar and changes the hero photos without us.
approach.2: Gave the Carathéodory Museum and the Folklore Museum their own pages, each with its history and collection.
approach.3: Added a booking system for the Folklore Museum covering individual visits, group and school visits and guided tours, emailing the association and confirming to the visitor.

DKExecutive.title: Chauffeured transfers and tours across Athens, booked in four steps
DKExecutive.summary: A bilingual site for DK Executive, a luxury transfer service in Athens: six services, seven tours and a Mercedes fleet, all leading into one booking form.
DKExecutive.challenge: DK Executive drives visitors around Athens around the clock, from airport pickups and weddings to corporate hire and day trips to Delphi, Meteora and Cape Sounion. Most of its customers are travellers booking from abroad, often from a phone, so the site had to read in English and Greek, show the fleet honestly, and take a full journey (pickup, drop-off, flight number, passengers) without a back-and-forth by email.

approach.0: Built the whole site in English and Greek, with its own route and metadata per language.
approach.1: Designed a four-step booking form (itinerary, vehicle, details, confirm) covering transfers, tours and hourly disposal.
approach.2: Used the Google Maps API to autocomplete pickup and drop-off addresses, so every request arrives with a real location.
approach.3: Gave each of the six services and seven tours, from Athens by Night to Meteora, its own page ending in the same booking flow, and laid out the five Mercedes vehicles by passenger count.

Principal.title: A wedding hall, an estate and 9,000 meals a day, on one site
Principal.summary: A bilingual site for Principal, a wedding hall and catering company in Orestiada: two venues, four catering services, its certifications and international registrations, all leading to one quote form.
Principal.challenge: Principal has catered in Evros since 2007 and does two quite different jobs from the same kitchen: weddings and receptions at its 700-guest hall and 1,000-guest estate, and contract catering (school meals, industrial catering, operational support) with a capacity of 9,000 meals a day. A couple choosing a venue and a procurement officer vetting a supplier both had to find what they came for, in Greek and English, and reach the company with one request.

approach.0: Built the whole site in Greek and English, with its own route and metadata per language.
approach.1: Presented the Principal Hall and the Principal Estate side by side on a venues page, each with its capacity and setting, so a couple can compare indoors and outdoors at a glance.
approach.2: Laid out the four services (school meals, industrial catering, event catering and operational support) on a page of their own, so institutional buyers aren't reading a wedding brochure.
approach.3: Gave the ISO 9001, ISO 45001 and ISO 27001 certifications and the D-U-N-S, NCAGE and SAM registrations their own pages, so a buyer can check the company's credentials directly.
approach.4: Kept an “Ask for a Quote” button in the navigation of every page, leading to one form that takes the event date and type, so each request arrives with what the team needs to price it.

Evresis.title: Property across northern Evros, searched from one bar
Evresis.summary: A bilingual site for Evresis, a real estate agency in Orestiada: homes, commercial spaces and land for sale and rent, alongside the office's print works and building management. Currently in development.
Evresis.challenge: Evresis sells and lets homes, commercial spaces and land in Nea Orestiada, Didymoteicho, Soufli and the villages of northern Evros, and runs a print works and a building management service from the same office. The site has to let a buyer or tenant narrow the portfolio by area, type and price in one step, give the two other services room of their own, and leave the agency able to publish and retire listings without a developer.

approach.0: Built the whole site in Greek and English, with its own route and metadata per language.
approach.1: Put one search bar in the hero (sale or rent, area, property type, price range), so the portfolio is filtered before the first scroll.
approach.2: Set that search over a Mapbox map of Orestiada, so the agency's own streets are the first thing a visitor sees.
approach.3: Modelled the listings in Sanity, so the agency adds, edits and retires properties itself.
approach.4: Gave the print works and building management their own pages, so the office's two other services aren't buried under the listings.

aboutPage.title: A small studio that designs and builds.
aboutPage.intro: codeloop is run by Stefanos Topsidis, a web designer and developer based in Athens, Greece, working remotely with clients across Greece and abroad.
aboutPage.whoBody: One person does the design and the code, with specialists brought in for photography, copy or illustration when a project needs them. That is deliberate: the usual gap between an agency's designer and its developer is where detail gets lost and timelines slip. Here the person who drew the page is the person who ships it.

0.q: How much does a website cost?
0.a: Most marketing sites we build land between $5k and $15k. E-shops, booking sites and web apps start higher because of the integrations. The brief asks for a budget range and we scope the project to fit it, rather than quoting a number and squeezing the work afterwards.

1.a: A design-and-build engagement runs six to twelve weeks. If the scope is unclear, a two-week discovery sprint comes first and ends with a fixed estimate. Small sites can launch in a month.

2.q: Do you work with clients outside Athens?
2.a: Yes. The studio is based in Athens, Greece, and works remotely with businesses across Greece and abroad, in English and Greek. Meetings happen on video, and progress is reviewed on a live preview link.

3.q: What do you build websites with?
3.a: Next.js, React and TypeScript, with Tailwind for styling and Sanity as the headless CMS. Sites are hosted on Vercel. The result is a site that loads fast, scores well on Core Web Vitals and does not need plugin updates.

4.q: Can I update the site myself after launch?
4.a: Yes. Text, images, pages, products and prices are edited in the CMS without touching code. Every build ends with a short training session and a written guide.

5.a: Technical SEO is part of every build: semantic HTML, titles and descriptions per page and language, structured data, a sitemap, hreflang for the two languages, and performance tuned for mobile. Content strategy and ongoing SEO can be added through the partner engagement.

6.a: Every site we ship for a Greek business is built in Greek and English, with separate URLs, metadata and content per language, so each version can rank on its own.

7.a: You get a handover: the code, the CMS, the hosting account and the design files, plus training. If you want continued support, the ongoing partner engagement reserves monthly capacity for updates and new pages.
